clue.text: Starting new climb

blocks.note: N is the standard abbreviation for new
an ascent is a climb

explanation.surface: Someone is beginning a fresh climb up a mountain.
explanation.definitionFit: Something nascent is just coming into being, so it is beginning or starting out.

clue.text: First lieutenant, that's me ...

blocks.note: first meaning: naval slang for a ship's second-in-command
second meaning: informal for oneself, looking after one's own interests

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis runs on into the next clue but adds nothing to the parse. In the Royal Navy the first lieutenant is the executive officer.
explanation.definitionFit: Naval slang names the executive officer this way, and the phrase is also an informal term for oneself.

clue.text: ... whereas the engineers are Frank and Ernest, by the sound of it

definitions.text: Frank and Ernest, by the sound of it

blocks.note: since can mean whereas, as in giving a reason
RE is the Royal Engineers, the British Army's engineering corps

explanation.surface: Continuing the previous clue, the engineers are two men named Frank and Ernest.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank and Ernest look like names; say them and they are the adjectives frank and earnest. RE is the Royal Engineers.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone sincere speaks honestly and means it, being both open and serious in what they say.

clue.text: Running away from constituent who is out of work

indicators.note: being out of something here means sitting outside it, so the constituent wraps around the work

blocks.note: an element is a constituent part
OP is short for opus, a musical work

explanation.surface: A voter who has lost their job is fleeing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Constituent' suggests a voter and 'out of work' unemployment; instead they are a component and a containment, with the work sitting inside. OP is the usual abbreviation for opus.
explanation.definitionFit: An elopement is the act of running off secretly to marry, usually without parental consent.

clue.text: Turned up to touch for some brass

indicators.note: in a down clue, turning a word upwards reads it from bottom to top

blocks.note: to abut is to touch along a border

explanation.surface: Someone arrived to cadge some money from a contact.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Brass' is British slang for money, but here it is the brass section of an orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The tuba is the largest, lowest-pitched instrument of the brass family, so it is one example of brass.

clue.text: The Pool of London secure

blocks.note: Jack London was the American author of The Call of the Wild
to pot something is to bag or secure it, as a hunter pots game

explanation.surface: The Pool of London, a stretch of the Thames below London Bridge, is being made safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The Pool of London' reads as one place name, but it splits: the definition is 'The Pool', and 'of London' is the writer's first name.
explanation.definitionFit: A jackpot is the accumulated pool of prize money in a lottery or card game.

clue.text: Flag conveying to marine “message understood"

blocks.note: Jolly is old naval slang for a Royal Marine
roger is radio code for message received and understood

explanation.surface: A signal flag passes an acknowledgement to a marine.
explanation.walkthrough: A Jolly is the Royal Navy's slang for a Royal Marine.
explanation.definitionFit: The Jolly Roger is the black pirate banner bearing a skull and crossbones.

clue.text: Jazz fan attached to church music

blocks.note: cat is old jazz slang for an enthusiast
CH is the standard abbreviation for church

explanation.surface: A jazz lover is devoted to sacred music.
explanation.definitionFit: A catch is a type of round for several voices, often comic, popular in England in the seventeenth century.

clue.text: College servant holding message up — and it's for the head!

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the message word is read from the bottom
holding something keeps it inside, so the servant wraps around the message

blocks.note: gip, more often gyp, is a college servant at Cambridge
a wire is a telegram, a short message

explanation.surface: A college porter brings a telegram upstairs, and it is meant for the headmaster.
explanation.walkthrough: The servant word and its contents are both reversed in the grid: GIP reads PIG upwards. 'Head' suggests the head of college, but it is a literal head.
explanation.definitionFit: A periwig is a powdered wig of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, worn over the head.

clue.text: After he left they all came in to the reckoning

indicators.note: after something has left it is gone, so those letters are taken out
coming in means going inside, so the second word is placed within the first

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letters removed
taken as written

explanation.surface: Once one man departed, the rest entered for the final count.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Left' looks like the past of leave in the story, and so it is: the man departs from the word, and the remaining two letters take in the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A tally is a running count or score, the total reckoned up so far.

clue.text: Saki's mountain

definitions.note: a possessive standing for a noun, fair because the 's is read as 'Saki is', giving the writer's real surname

blocks.note: first meaning: the real surname of the writer Saki
second meaning: a Scottish peak over 3,000 feet

explanation.walkthrough: Saki's possessive is read as 'Saki is': the short-story writer's real name was Hector Hugh Munro.
explanation.definitionFit: Saki was the pen name of Hector Hugh Munro, and Scottish peaks above three thousand feet are called Munros after the man who listed them.

clue.text: Art liable to be split between two parties

indicators.note: something split is broken apart, so the letters of the preceding words are pulled apart and rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A painting is likely to be divided up between two owners.
explanation.definitionFit: A bilateral agreement or treaty is one made between two sides, from the Latin for two-sided.

clue.text: Team comes out of the tunnel eventually

indicators.note: what comes out of something was inside it, so the letters emerge from within the following words

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of tunnel and the start of eventually

explanation.surface: A football side finally emerges from the players' tunnel onto the pitch.
explanation.definitionFit: Football and cricket sides each have this many players, so the number names the team itself.

clue.text: Minor road for each to enter in passing

indicators.note: one part going in to the other means it is placed inside the minor road

blocks.note: a byway is a minor road
'the' can mean per, as in a pound the kilo

explanation.surface: A side road where each traveller can join the traffic, as directions might explain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The' meaning each is the shopkeeper's usage, as in fifty pence the pound.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase introduces an incidental remark, made casually or as an aside, which is what saying something in passing means.

clue.text: Tie pin came adrift, causing irritability

indicators.note: something adrift has come loose from its moorings, so the letters float into a new order

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: A tie-pin worked loose, which made its wearer annoyed.
explanation.definitionFit: Impatience is restless intolerance of delay or annoyance, closely akin to being easily irritated.

clue.text: Flower with neat look

blocks.note: neat is an old word for cattle, and an ox is one such beast
to eye something is to look at it

explanation.surface: A flower with a tidy appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: Neat here is the old noun for cattle, not the adjective for tidy.
explanation.definitionFit: The ox-eye daisy is a common wild plant with large white petals around a yellow centre.

clue.text: It could disperse thin gloom

indicators.note: dispersing scatters things, so the letters of the last two words are scattered and regathered

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Something that might lift a faint darkness at night.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both the wordplay and the definition: the light from a full moon does lift a thin darkness.
explanation.definitionFit: Light reflected from the moon brightens the night, so it can dispel a faint darkness.

clue.text: Dug a rifle out, being responsible for safety on beach

definitions.text: being responsible for safety on beach

indicators.note: out suggests something put out of order, so the preceding letters are rearranged

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Someone got a gun out, saying they were in charge of keeping the beach safe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Being' reads as a verb, but it is a noun: a person who is responsible for bathers' safety.
explanation.definitionFit: A lifeguard is a person employed to watch over swimmers and rescue anyone in difficulty in the water.

clue.text: Ropy decoration for an Aga?

blocks.note: first meaning: an ornamental knot worked in rope
second meaning: what an Ottoman commander has on his shoulders

explanation.walkthrough: An Aga is a British range cooker, but here it is the Ottoman title for a commander, so his head belongs to a Turk.
explanation.definitionFit: This ornamental knot looks like a turban, and an aga, being a Turkish officer, has such a head.

clue.text: Emigrant has no right to dwell on

indicators.note: having none of something means it is taken away from the word for emigrant

blocks.note: an expatriate has left their own country to live abroad
R is the standard abbreviation for right

explanation.surface: Someone who has emigrated has lost the right to stay somewhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dwell' looks like the emigrant's residence, but 'dwell on' is the definition: to talk at length.
explanation.definitionFit: To expatiate is to speak or write at great length about a subject, lingering over it in detail.

clue.text: Game of bridge

blocks.note: first meaning: a card game also called twenty-one or blackjack
second meaning: a floating support for a temporary crossing

explanation.walkthrough: 'Game of bridge' reads as one card game; bridge here is a structure across a river.
explanation.definitionFit: Pontoon is the British name for the card game twenty-one, and a pontoon is also a floating bridge.

clue.text: Fell for captivating look

indicators.note: to captivate is to take captive, so one word holds the other inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
lo is an old exclamation meaning look

explanation.surface: Someone was charmed by an attractive appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fell for' reads as falling in love, but 'Fell' alone is the definition, a verb meaning knock down; lo is an archaic exclamation meaning look.
explanation.definitionFit: To fell an opponent and to floor them both mean knocking them to the ground.

clue.text: Go and talk about gym

indicators.note: about means around, so the talk word wraps around the gym word

blocks.note: to orate is to talk pompously or give a speech
PE is physical education, school gym lessons

explanation.surface: Someone sets off to give a lecture on gymnastics.
explanation.walkthrough: PE is physical education, the British school subject; 'Go' is the definition in the sense of a machine working.
explanation.definitionFit: A machine that goes is working, and to operate likewise means to function or run.

clue.text: Chinese fruit

blocks.note: first meaning: the standard spoken language of China
second meaning: a small loose-skinned orange

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a fruit from China; the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names the main spoken language of China and a small citrus fruit like a tangerine.

clue.text: The idea of doctor becoming inverted

indicators.note: inverted means turned upside down, which in a down clue reads the becoming word upwards

blocks.note: MO is a medical officer, an army doctor
becoming means suitable or fit

explanation.surface: The notion of a physician turning upside down.
explanation.definitionFit: A motif is a recurring theme in a work of art or music, a central dominant idea.

clue.text: For instance, a bird seen in a tree

blocks.note: as can mean for instance, as in big cats such as lions
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: An example of a bird spotted perched in a tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen in' suggests one part inside another, but it only joins wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The aspen is a poplar tree whose leaves tremble in the slightest breeze.

clue.text: Worsted in retreat, rebels finally on the way out

indicators.note: a retreating army goes back the way it came, so this word runs backwards
finally points to the very end of the word rebels

blocks.note: serge is a hard-wearing worsted fabric
the closing letter of rebels

explanation.surface: Beaten and falling back, the rebels are finally leaving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Worsted' reads as 'defeated', but here it is the woollen cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: Egress is a formal word for an exit, the passage by which one leaves a place.

clue.text: Admiral executed a singer, they say

indicators.note: what people say is heard rather than read, so the singer's name is taken by its spoken form

blocks.note: Bing Crosby was the American crooner

explanation.surface: An admiral put a performer to death, so the story goes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Executed' looks like an action the admiral took, but he was the one shot: Admiral John Byng was executed in 1757 for failing at Minorca.
explanation.definitionFit: Admiral John Byng was court-martialled and shot by firing squad on his own quarterdeck in 1757.

clue.text: Worth almost nothing, pay went on being reduced

indicators.note: something reduced is broken down, so the preceding words are broken into letters and rebuilt

blocks.note: the fodder, taken letter for letter

explanation.surface: Wages that kept being cut ended up worth very little.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes things so common and cheap that they could be bought two for a single penny.

clue.text: A cereal -- no one bowl over

indicators.note: no signals that the following item is left out of the cereal

blocks.note: taken as written
maize is a cereal crop
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A breakfast cereal that no one would serve in a bowl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' looks like the dish for cereal; 'bowl over' is the definition, meaning astonish.
explanation.definitionFit: To bowl someone over is to astonish them completely, which is to astound or stun them.

clue.text: About a quarter intended to provide money

indicators.note: about means around, so the intended word goes around the quarter

blocks.note: one's intended is one's betrothed
north is one quarter of the compass

explanation.surface: Roughly a quarter of the sum is meant to cover expenses.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Intended' looks like a verb, but it is a noun: the person one is engaged to. A quarter is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: To finance a project is to fund it, supplying the cash it needs.

clue.text: Start to get curious about foreign money in unexpected windfall

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter
about means around, so the curious word wraps the foreign money

blocks.note: the opening letter of get
odd means strange or curious
the sen is a small coin of Japan and other Asian countries

explanation.surface: Taking an interest in overseas currency leads to a surprising stroke of luck.
explanation.walkthrough: The sen is a hundredth of a Japanese yen, a favourite crossword coin.
explanation.definitionFit: A godsend is a welcome stroke of luck arriving out of the blue, as if sent from heaven.
